past_medical_history: Bilateral lung transplant 4 months ago — indication: COPD end-stage

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Intact. No facial weakness. No ptosis.
neurological_exam.motor: Lower extremity weakness: hip flexion 3/5 bilaterally, knee extension 3/5, ankle dorsiflexion 3/5. Cannot walk without support. Upper extremity: normal (5/5).
neurological_exam.sensory: No sensory deficits at initial presentation. Mild distal tingling reported at 2-week follow-up.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Initially (week 1): deep tendon reflexes normal (2+) throughout. Week 3: hypoactive patellar (1+), absent Achilles bilaterally.
neurological_exam.coordination: Intact upper extremities. Lower extremities limited by weakness.
neurological_exam.gait: Progressive inability to ambulate — requires bilateral support. Started with dizziness and difficulty 2 weeks ago; now cannot walk.
neurological_exam.additional: Tacrolimus trough levels: target 8-12 ng/mL; average 10.5 ± 4.1 ng/mL over 3 months. No history of tacrolimus toxicity (no elevated levels). No recent infections, immunizations, or new medications. CMV PCR serum: negative. EBV PCR serum: negative. Brain MRI: normal. Insidious onset over 2 weeks, with total disease duration of approximately 4 weeks.

patient.chief_complaint: Two-week progressive lower extremity weakness with dizziness and difficulty walking, 4 months after bilateral lung transplant on triple immunosuppression.
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. F. is a 66-year-old bilateral lung transplant recipient presenting 4 months post-transplant with a 2-week history of progressive lower extremity weakness. He underwent uncomplicated bilateral lung transplantation 4 months ago for end-stage COPD. His immunosuppression regimen is tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone, with tacrolimus levels consistently therapeutic at 10.5 ng/mL on average over 3 months. He reports no recent infections, new medications, immunizations, or exposures. He denies respiratory illness or diarrheal illness. Two weeks ago he began noticing dizziness and generalized weakness with difficulty ambulating. The weakness has been specifically in his lower extremities and has progressed gradually — he initially needed a cane and now requires bilateral support. He has no upper extremity weakness and no sensory symptoms initially, though mild distal tingling developed in the second week. He initially had normal reflexes on exam, which became hypoactive and then absent at the ankles by week 3. The subacute 2-3 week progression on triple immunosuppression raised concern for a tacrolimus-related polyneuropathy (tacrolimus can cause demyelinating neuropathy), though levels are therapeutic. CMV and EBV (common post-transplant opportunistic infections) were tested and are negative.

quantitative_data.pattern: Acute demyelinating polyneuropathy with axonal changes — acquired demyelinating pattern, distinct from a length-dependent toxic/metabolic polyneuropathy

specialized_test.impression: Acute demyelinating polyneuropathy with axonal features. Increased distal motor latencies, reduced conduction velocities, decreased CMAP amplitudes, absent F-waves and H-reflexes bilaterally. Asymmetric left greater than right involvement. Reduced sural and ulnar sensory SNAP amplitudes. Findings meet electrodiagnostic criteria for acute demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy

cardiac_monitoring.rhythm_summary: Sinus rhythm with recurrent sinus bradycardia to 42 bpm and two sinus pauses of 3.2 and 3.8 seconds, both during tracheal suctioning; alternating sinus tachycardia to 138 bpm

events.description: During tracheal suctioning; asymptomatic, resolved spontaneously
During suctioning; prompted atropine at the bedside and continued ICU monitoring
Systolic swings from 178 to 96 mmHg without postural change

findings: Recurrent sinus bradycardia with pauses greater than 3 seconds
Blood-pressure lability without a postural trigger
No sustained tachyarrhythmia and no AV block
cardiac_monitoring.impression: Continuous inpatient telemetry through the period of maximal weakness. Autonomic instability is present in about two thirds of patients with Guillain-Barré syndrome and is a leading cause of in-hospital death, so this recording is a monitoring requirement rather than a diagnostic test: it detects the bradyarrhythmias, pauses and blood-pressure lability that trigger ICU escalation, alongside serial respiratory function. Pauses beyond 3 seconds with blood-pressure lability constitute significant dysautonomia: continuous monitoring is maintained, atropine kept at the bedside, and suctioning treated as a provocative manoeuvre.

output.proposed: IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day x 5 days in post-lung transplant patient on tacrolimus/MMF/prednisone
interactions: IVIG + tacrolimus: no direct pharmacokinetic interaction; sucrose-based IVIG can cause renal impairment — use non-sucrose formulation given baseline Cr 1.4

contraindications: Plasmapheresis in post-transplant patient: may rapidly clear tacrolimus leading to rejection risk — IVIG strongly preferred over plasmapheresis in organ transplant recipients
warnings: Do NOT reduce tacrolimus without transplant team — rejection risk is high; GBS treatment is IVIG, not tacrolimus reduction
Non-sucrose IVIG formulation preferred given baseline renal impairment from tacrolimus
alternatives: Plasmapheresis is CONTRAINDICATED in solid organ transplant — clears immunosuppressive medications; IVIG is the only appropriate treatment

general.summary: No directly applicable, high-quality evidence was retrieved for this query. Recommend correlating with current society guidelines.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Guillain-Barré syndrome, AIDP (post-lung transplant, likely immune dysregulation)

differential.key_features: Encephalopathy, tremor, and seizures more typical; chronic length-dependent neuropathy possible; trough levels and dose review.

differential.diagnosis: Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease with CNS / nerve involvement
differential.key_features: EBV PCR, imaging, and CSF cytology; pattern typically focal rather than symmetric ascending.
Common opportunistic post-transplant; CSF CMV PCR and serum CMV PCR; usually marked CSF neutrophilic pleocytosis.
Post-transplant ICU course increases risk; symmetric ascending pattern less typical.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain CBC, CMP, HIV, anti-GM1/anti-GQ1b ganglioside antibodies, and stool culture / Campylobacter serology if recent diarrhea
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Mild leukocytosis / elevated inflammatory markers reflecting antecedent infection; ganglioside antibodies for variant typing; trigger identification (Campylobacter, CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma, HIV)

optimal_actions.action: Order nerve conduction studies and needle EMG (EMG/NCS)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Demyelinating pattern (prolonged DML, conduction block, reduced CV, absent F-waves) consistent with AIDP, or reduced CMAP amplitudes in axonal variants (AMAN/AMSAN)

optimal_actions.action: Perform lumbar puncture for CSF analysis
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Albuminocytologic dissociation — elevated protein with cell count <10/μL; may be normal in the first week of illness

optimal_actions.action: Order bedside respiratory function testing (FVC, MIP/MEP, NIF) and repeat every 4–6 hours
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Baseline and serial FVC, MIP/MEP, NIF; deterioration to FVC <20 mL/kg, MIP worse than -30 cmH2O, or VC <40% predicted triggers ICU transfer / intubation

optimal_actions.action: Search the medical literature for IVIG vs plasma exchange evidence to guide disease-modifying therapy
optimal_actions.expected_finding: IVIG (0.4 g/kg/day x 5 days) and plasma exchange are equivalently effective first-line therapies; combination not superior

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions / contraindications for IVIG (renal function, IgA deficiency screen) and/or plasma exchange (coagulation, calcium, hemodynamics)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Confirmation that IVIG can be given safely (no severe renal impairment, no IgA deficiency) or that plasma exchange is appropriate (adequate vascular access, stable coagulation)

optimal_actions.action: Obtain a 12-lead ECG to screen for autonomic dysrhythmias and baseline QTc
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sinus tachycardia or bradycardia; conduction or repolarisation abnormalities reflecting autonomic involvement

optimal_actions.action: Start continuous inpatient cardiac telemetry for the period of maximal weakness and keep it running alongside serial respiratory function. Autonomic instability affects about two thirds of patients and is a leading cause of in-hospital death: bradyarrhythmias, pauses beyond 3 seconds and blood-pressure lability are what trigger ICU escalation
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Documentation of sinus pauses, bradyarrhythmias, BP lability, or non-sustained tachyarrhythmias

useless_tools.rationale: GBS is a peripheral nerve / nerve-root disorder; EEG has no role in diagnosis unless atypical CNS features (encephalopathy, seizures) are present.
Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Head CT contributes no diagnostic information in GBS; the disease is peripheral and CT does not visualise nerve roots reliably.
Brain MRI is reserved for atypical features (encephalopathy, CNS signs, transverse myelitis on differential). In classic GBS it does not aid diagnosis.

sequence_constraints.reason: Document respiratory status (FVC/NIF) before committing to IVIG vs plasma exchange — severe respiratory compromise mandates ICU triage and may influence treatment choice and timing.
Renal function, IgA screen, and CBC must be reviewed before IVIG to mitigate renal failure, anaphylaxis (IgA-deficient patients), and aseptic meningitis risk.

critical_actions: Coordinate with transplant team — adjust immunosuppression cautiously.
Initiate IVIG (preferred over plasma exchange in immunocompromised transplant recipient).
CMV PCR (serum and CSF) and EBV PCR given transplant status.
Pharmacology review for nephrotoxic and neurotoxic interactions.
contraindicated_actions: Do not discontinue immunosuppression abruptly — rejection risk.
Do not give corticosteroids as monotherapy in GBS (they are part of baseline transplant regimen but not specifically for GBS).
key_reasoning_points: Solid-organ transplant recipients have multiple competing causes for new neuropathy — opportunistic infection, drug toxicity, PTLD — but GBS still occurs and remains diagnosable on the same Brighton criteria.
IVIG is generally preferred over PLEX in transplant recipients to avoid removing therapeutic immunosuppressant levels.
Coordinate medication review with transplant pharmacy — CNI and IVIG interaction, renal status.

red_herrings.data_point: Recent lung transplant with multiple immunosuppressants
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on calcineurin-inhibitor toxicity or opportunistic infection rather than GBS.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Classic Brighton-level clinical pattern (areflexia, ascending weakness, CSF albuminocytologic dissociation, demyelinating EMG) defines GBS even in transplant recipients; opportunistic causes must be excluded but do not preclude the diagnosis.

Agents calling order_specialized_test{respiratory_function} will hit the EMG/NCS output instead.
